target_customer: Consumers wanting to track stress and anxiety with a wearable armband
problem: People cannot easily notice or manage rising stress, so a wearable reading heart rate variability alerts them and suggests ways to reduce it.
business_model: Consumer hardware sales with companion app

technical_complexity.rationale: Reliable passive stress sensing from heart rate variability, plus the original claim of nutrition tracking by spectroscopy, needs hardware, signal processing and validation; the nutrition claims drew skepticism.

defensibility.rationale: No patents or validation found; many wearables measured heart rate variability, so stress tracking was copyable.

takeover_risk_then.outcome: General fitness wearables added stress features later; Airo did not ship the original device.

market_need_then: Interest in wearables was high in 2013 to 2014 (84 million trackers sold in 2013 per IHS data cited by Smithsonian) and Spire showed demand for stress tracking, but no Airo purchase data was found.

identity.visual_style: 2013 design described as a unibody bead-blasted aluminum cuff with a soft matte finish
identity.voice_and_tone: Health and calm messaging; later positioned on anxiety rather than nutrition

branding.community_and_virality: Wide 2013 launch coverage (Engadget, Business Insider, BetaKit) followed by skepticism from MobiHealthNews and refunds to preorder backers

brand_strength.rationale: Strong initial press reach, but credibility damage from the questioned nutrition claim and the cancelled preorders undermined it.

pivots.from: Multi-sensor wristband tracking nutrition, stress, exercise and sleep
pivots.to: Armband focused on anxiety and stress
pivots.why: Original calorie and nutrition claims drew skepticism and preorders were cancelled for further testing; exact date not found

outcome_analysis: Airo launched in 2013 with a wristband promising passive nutrition and stress tracking, and its claims drew skepticism, after which it cancelled preorders for further testing and refunded backers. It later joined Y Combinator Summer 2016 with an anxiety focused armband and about $120K reported funding, but YC lists it inactive and no source states a shutdown or its date. The cancelled preorders and narrowing of the product suggest the core sensing claim was not delivered, which is recorded as tech unsolved with that caveat.
